newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE - Erstwhile angel Cavallo bedevils government.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Erstwhile angel Cavallo bedevils government.

text.p: He was the angel of financial markets until Argentine President Carlos Menem clipped his wings and cast him from the cabinet for picking one too many fights.
Now, three months out of the economy ministry, Domingo Cavallo is back and bedevilling his former cabinet colleagues with headline-grabbing allegations of corruption.
The former "superminister", now dabbling as a lecturer, economic adviser and even a newspaper columnist, is also on the campaign trail.

After seven years in government as a technocrat with no party affiliation, 50-year-old Cavallo has declared his intention to run for Congress in elections next year but not for the ruling Peronists or the two main opposition parties.
Much to the dismay of officialdom, his barbs at the government have kept his profile as high as when he ran the ministry facing the "Pink House" presidential palace.

After serving two years as foreign minister, Cavallo moved to the economy post in 1991, pegging the peso to the dollar under a reform plan that helped slash inflation from 5,000 percent to zero and won the adulation of investors and monetary authorities abroad.
BECAME POLITICAL LIABILITY

Long considered an economic necessity, he recently became a political liability for his combative style and austerity policies at a time of 17 percent unemployment, fuelling anger from the public, church, labour and political opponents.
On July 29, tired of the clashes with himself, cabinet members and the ruling party's old guard, Menem jettisoned his blue-eyed Harvard-trained economist.
Both Cavallo and his wife Sonia publicly welcomed the move as an opportunity to slow down. It was a short-lived rest.
Cavallo, taking most of his top aides with him, went six blocks down the road from his old office, rented space in a press building and set to work making money and plans to return to power.

He has since served as an economic adviser to the new government of Ecuadorean President Abdala Bucaram, gives lectures for $25,000 each and committed himself to writing a column for Italy's La Stampa.
In a recent two-week period, Cavallo had commitments taking him to Brazil, Peru, Ecuador, Argentina, Venezuela and the United States.
But his regular front-page appearance in newspapers is based on a corruption crusade with allegations that his enemies say are politically driven.
Government officials have denounced him as no less than a traitor, a "political cannibal" and "emotionally unstable."
He publicly alleged that Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan had manipulated judges and covered up corruption in government.

He also accused presidential Chief of Staff Alberto Kohan of knowing that bribes were paid in a $250 million contract to upgrade computers at Argentina's biggest bank. Eleven former IBM Argentina and Banco Nacion employees have been indicted.
The government has denied all the charges.
The attacks, said political analyst Julio Blanck, were akin to guerrilla-like strikes.
"He chooses the moment of attack and selects his targets," he said. "He makes a surprise strike and withdraws."
LAWSUITS PENDING
In the process, Cavallo may well have earned the distinction of facing the most lawsuits in the land.
Corach grumbled that Cavallo was "emotionally unstable", filed suit for slander and called for a three-year jail sentence.
Former customs chief Aldo Fuad Elias has also taken legal action following Cavallo's allegations that he did nothing against mafias in customs.
Kohan has threatened to sue as well. Cavallo already had several lawsuits for similar accusations pending.
Asked whether Cavallo betrayed the government, Kohan sniffed: "No, one only betrays when one knows loyalty."
But Cavallo countered: "They will not shut my mouth. They don't want to let this citizen talk."
He acknowledges he has little proof, though, saying: "It is my word against that of the two ministers. It is a question of credibility."
Still, the ruling party bloc in Congress stopped an opposition plan to call Cavallo to testify to deprive him of a new platform to hurl accusations against the government.
Proof or not, Cavallo still carries weight in the markets, which have hung on his words.

"If the political landscape doesn't change it may be tough for the market," said Horacio Bonavia, trader for Portfolio brokers. "The market will keep an eye on Cavallo's agenda, where he goes, what he says."
Carlos Rodriguez, the chief economic adviser to Cavallo's successor Roque Fernandez, said Cavallo's "political cannibalism" was damaging the country's image.
The president, stung by Cavallo's attacks, said his former aide had "passed to the opposition".

Asked about his political aspirations, Cavallo is coy. He has said his prickly style might not make him an ideal candidate for presidential polls in 1999. And he acknowledges he has a lot to learn about politics.
When questioned by a business audience in Brazil on whether he would run for president, he quipped: "I don't think I will be president because they will put me in jail before that."
